Consider a typical astronomical inference problem, the estimation of the physical properties of an exoplanet system from radial velocity and transit data. Such models often have 10 to 20 parameters, including planetary masses, radii, orbital periods, eccentricities and stellar properties. The posterior distribution of these parameters has complex correlations. It can also have several modes, which represent different valid solutions.

Chapter 12 introduced the grid method, the inverse CDF method, rejection sampling and importance sampling. Each of them suffers from some form of the curse of dimensionality, where the computing requirements grow exponentially with the number of parameters. They reach practical limits for the complex, high-dimensional problems of modern astronomy.

With 10 parameters and 100 grid points per dimension, a grid needs \(10^{20}\) evaluations. Inverse transform sampling faces a different challenge, because computing and inverting the cumulative distribution function is analytically intractable for complex posteriors. Rejection sampling suffers from exponentially decreasing acceptance rates as the dimension increases. Even importance sampling has difficulty finding proposal distributions that adequately cover high-dimensional parameter spaces.

This chapter introduces Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), a family of algorithms that overcome these dimensionality limits. They have transformed Bayesian inference in astronomy over the past three decades. Unlike the global approaches of Chapter 12, it moves through the parameter space in sequential, local steps. The sequence of positions that it visits is called a chain. Each step depends only on the current position and not on the history of the chain. This local view is useful for the complex models of later chapters, where MCMC can support advanced techniques like Gaussian processes and neural networks.

The main idea is to construct a random walk through the parameter space instead of sampling directly from the posterior. A random walk is a path made of random steps. We design the rules of this random walk so that the chain eventually settles into a pattern that matches our target posterior distribution.

Imagine an explorer who wants to map the population distribution of Columbus, Ohio. A full census of the city would be analogous to a grid method. Instead, the explorer follows a simple strategy. Each day, the explorer randomly chooses a nearby neighborhood to visit, based only on the current location. The explorer chooses neighborhoods of higher population density more often.

At first, the explorer may wander somewhat randomly while learning about the city. After many days, a pattern emerges. The explorer spends more time in densely populated areas like the Short North and less time in sparse suburbs. The frequency of visits to each neighborhood eventually matches the true population distribution. Recording the daily locations over many weeks gives a representative sample of the population density of Columbus. We do not need a street-by-street survey.

In this strategy, the neighborhoods are points in our parameter space and the population density is the posterior probability. The explorer’s path is our Markov chain. Each day’s destination depends only on today’s location, and this sequential nature gives the method its name, Markov Chain Monte Carlo. Figure 13.1 shows a chain on a posterior with three modes.

MCMC has several advantages for astronomical applications. It needs to evaluate the posterior only up to a proportionality constant, so we avoid difficult normalization calculations. It handles correlations between parameters, because it moves through the parameter space step by step. It can discover and sample from multiple modes of the distribution when we design the algorithm appropriately. Most important, it scales to high dimensions, because it spends its computing effort on regions of high probability and does not attempt an exhaustive search.

MCMC also has difficulties that direct sampling does not have. The exploration is sequential, so successive samples are correlated with each other, which reduces their effective information content. We cannot observe directly whether the chain has converged to the target distribution (Section 13.4), so we need careful diagnostics (Section 13.13). The efficiency of the exploration depends on design choices of the algorithm, in particular on how we propose new moves through the parameter space.

13.1 Markov Chains and the Core Idea of MCMC

A process is Markovian when its future depends only on its present state, and not on how it reached that state. A state is one possible position of the process, such as a neighborhood in our analogy or a point in the parameter space. The set of possible states is the state space. The term comes from the Russian mathematician Andrey Markov, who studied such sequences of events. This “memoryless” property distinguishes Markov processes from processes in which the history matters.

In our Columbus analogy, the explorer visits one location each day, such as a café, a museum, a park or a neighborhood. A guidebook suggests where to go next, based only on the current location. The guidebook does not care whether the explorer came from downtown yesterday or from the suburbs last week. This selective memory defines the Markov property.

We denote the sequence of locations by \(\{X_0, X_1, X_2, \ldots\}\). The Markov property then says that \[ P(X_{t+1} = x | X_0 = x_0, X_1 = x_1, ..., X_t = x_t) = P(X_{t+1} = x | X_t = x_t). \]

The Markov property is computationally useful, because the transition probabilities between states are all we need to describe the system. The transition matrix \(T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\) determines the behavior of a Markov chain. It gives the probability density of moving to state \(\mathbf{x}'\) when the current state is \(\mathbf{x}\). In our analogy, \(T\) is the guidebook that gives the probability of visiting each location from the current one.

Suppose the explorer is in the Short North, an arts district. The guidebook might suggest a 40% chance of staying in the Short North, because it has many local attractions. It might suggest a 30% chance of moving to nearby German Village and a 20% chance of visiting downtown. The chance of traveling to more distant neighborhoods is 10%. These percentages sum to 100%, because the explorer ends each day in some neighborhood, possibly the same one. The transition probabilities from any state must therefore sum to 1, which is a requirement for any valid transition matrix.

We now follow all the people of Columbus instead of a single explorer. This shift from individual trajectories to population dynamics gives insight into how MCMC works. They move around the city according to the rules of our guidebook. Our goal is a guidebook for which the population distribution over the neighborhoods settles at a target distribution. The target could be the actual population density of Columbus. We then view the transition matrix \(T\) as an operator that transforms one population distribution into another.

The transition operator maps a distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) of people across the city to the distribution after everyone follows the guidebook for one step. It is defined by \[ (T p)(\mathbf{x'}) = \int p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x'}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}. \]

The quantity \((Tp)(\mathbf{x}')\) is the probability density of being at state \(\mathbf{x}'\) after applying the transition operator to \(p(\mathbf{x})\). The integral adds up all the ways of reaching \(\mathbf{x}'\) from any starting state \(\mathbf{x}\), each weighted by the probability of starting there. For a finite number of states, \(T\) is a matrix whose entry \(T(i,j)\) is the probability of moving from state \(i\) to state \(j\). We write \(p\) as a row of probabilities, so that \(Tp\) is the row \(p\) multiplied by the matrix \(T\) and \((Tp)(j) = \sum_i p(i)\,T(i,j)\).

How do we create a guidebook that leads to our desired distribution? We need a transition matrix for which the population distribution converges to the target and then stays there. We call a distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) stationary with respect to the transition operator \(T\) if applying \(T\) to \(p\) returns the same distribution \[ (T p)(\mathbf{x}) = p(\mathbf{x}). \]

In our analogy, suppose the population is already distributed according to the target distribution. When everyone follows the guidebook, the overall population distribution remains unchanged. The stationary distribution is the equilibrium state of our system.

Suppose now that we start with any initial distribution of people across Columbus. They follow the guidebook repeatedly. We want the population to redistribute itself to match the target pattern and then to stay that way. Once the population reaches this equilibrium, the flows of people balance. For each neighborhood, as many people arrive as leave. Figure 13.2(a) shows an initial distribution and the distribution after two steps, which is closer to the target distribution.

The central idea of MCMC connects the two viewpoints, the individual explorer and the population distribution. Suppose we design our guidebook so that the target posterior \(p(\mathbf{x}|\mathcal{D})\) is the stationary distribution of the resulting Markov chain. A single explorer who follows this guidebook for a long time then visits locations with frequencies proportional to their posterior probabilities. This link between the population and a single explorer relies on a principle called ergodicity, which we study in Section 13.5.

By recording where the explorer goes over many steps, we sample from the posterior distribution. We use these samples for the Bayesian calculations we need, such as computing posterior means, estimating uncertainties, making predictions and comparing models. This approach turns an intractable sampling problem into the design of a Markov chain with the right properties.

13.2 Detailed Balance

How do we construct a transition matrix whose stationary distribution is our target posterior? Detailed balance gives a practical condition for this. For clarity, we write the posterior \(p(\mathbf{x}|\mathcal{D})\) simply as \(p(\mathbf{x})\). It is the probability distribution of the model parameters \(\mathbf{x}\) given the observed data \(\mathcal{D}\).

Imagine that we want the Short North to have a bustling population and Upper Arlington to remain a quieter area. To achieve this distribution, our guidebook needs to encourage more people to move from Upper Arlington to the Short North than the other way around. Over time, the Short North population grows. As more people gather in the Short North, the population difference creates a counterbalance. There are more people in the Short North who might move to Upper Arlington, even if each person is less likely to move.

These opposing forces eventually reach equilibrium. People keep moving, and the flows between neighborhoods balance, so the population distribution stays constant. This balance occurs when the number of people moving from the Short North to Upper Arlington equals the number moving the other way. This condition is called detailed balance, and we write it as \[ p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x'}) = p(\mathbf{x'}) T(\mathbf{x'}, \mathbf{x}). \]

To read this equation, we interpret each term in our Columbus analogy. The quantity \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is the population of neighborhood \(\mathbf{x}\), here the Short North. The transition matrix \(T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\) is the probability that someone in the Short North moves to Upper Arlington, written \(\mathbf{x}'\). The left side \(p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\) is therefore the “flow” of people from the Short North to Upper Arlington.

The right side is the flow in the opposite direction. Detailed balance says that these two flows are equal for each pair of neighborhoods in our city. This is a strong condition. A stationary distribution only needs the total flow into each neighborhood to equal the total flow out of it. Figure 13.3 shows the two flows between a pair of states for a distribution on discrete states. Figure 13.2(b) shows these flows for two states during the approach to equilibrium.

Detailed balance gives us a concrete way to design the transition matrix. We can evaluate the target distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) up to a constant, because the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. We can therefore use \(p(\mathbf{x})\) to construct a guidebook that leads to this distribution.

We now prove that detailed balance makes \(p(\mathbf{x})\) a stationary distribution. We must show that, if detailed balance holds, then \(p(\mathbf{x})\) satisfies the stationary distribution equation \[ p(\mathbf{x'}) = \int p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x'}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}. \]

We integrate both sides of the detailed balance equation over all states \(\mathbf{x}\) \[\begin{aligned} \int p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x'}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} &= \int p(\mathbf{x'}) T(\mathbf{x'}, \mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}. \end{aligned}\]

On the right side, \(p(\mathbf{x}')\) does not depend on \(\mathbf{x}\), so we can move it outside the integral \[\begin{aligned} \int p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x'}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} &= p(\mathbf{x'}) \int T(\mathbf{x'}, \mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}. \end{aligned}\]

The integral \(\int T(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}\) equals 1, because the probabilities of moving from state \(\mathbf{x}'\) to all possible states sum to 1. In our analogy, the probabilities of moving from Upper Arlington to all neighborhoods, including staying in Upper Arlington, add up to 100%.

We therefore obtain \[ \int p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x'}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} = p(\mathbf{x'}) \cdot 1 = p(\mathbf{x'}). \]

This is the definition of a stationary distribution. If detailed balance holds, the target distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is therefore a stationary distribution of the Markov chain with transition matrix \(T\). In our analogy, balanced flows between any two neighborhoods keep the population of each neighborhood constant.

This gives us a practical strategy for constructing MCMC algorithms. We design transition matrices that satisfy detailed balance with respect to our target posterior distribution. The task is then to construct transition rules that balance the flows between neighborhoods.

13.3 The Metropolis Algorithm

Many approaches in the MCMC literature construct such transition rules. The Metropolis algorithm is the simplest and most intuitive solution. It shows that a suitable transition matrix exists and gives a simple way to construct it.

In the Metropolis algorithm, we split the transition into two steps. First we propose a new state, and then we decide whether to accept or reject the proposal. In our analogy, the explorer first consults a guidebook that suggests a neighborhood to visit, which is the proposal. The explorer then decides personally whether to follow the suggestion, which is the acceptance or rejection step. This two-step process lets us design a transition mechanism that satisfies detailed balance.

We write the transition matrix as \[ T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = q(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}) A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}'), \] where \(q(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x})\) is the proposal distribution and \(A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\) is the acceptance probability of the proposed move. The proposal distribution is the probability density of suggesting a move to state \(\mathbf{x}'\) when we are at state \(\mathbf{x}\). The formula for \(T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\) holds for \(\mathbf{x}' \neq \mathbf{x}\), because a rejected proposal keeps the chain at \(\mathbf{x}\) and adds the probability of rejection to \(T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x})\).

The Metropolis algorithm requires a symmetric proposal distribution, which means that \[ q(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}) = q(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{x}'). \]

In our analogy, the guidebook is as likely to suggest a trip from the Short North to Upper Arlington as the reverse trip. A common example in astronomical applications is a multivariate Gaussian centered at the current position \[ q(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}), \] where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the covariance matrix. The matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) controls the step size and direction of our proposals. This proposal is symmetric, because the distance from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{x}'\) is the same as the distance from \(\mathbf{x}'\) to \(\mathbf{x}\).

For this symmetric proposal, the Metropolis algorithm defines the acceptance probability as \[ A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})}\right). \]

Suppose the proposed state \(\mathbf{x}'\) has a higher posterior probability than the current state \(\mathbf{x}\), so that \(p(\mathbf{x}') \geq p(\mathbf{x})\). The ratio \(p(\mathbf{x}')/p(\mathbf{x})\) is then at least 1, and we accept the proposal with probability 1. If the proposed state has a lower posterior probability, so that \(p(\mathbf{x}') < p(\mathbf{x})\), the ratio is below 1. We then accept the proposal with a probability equal to this ratio. For example, if the proposed state has 70% of the probability density of the current state, we accept the move with 70% probability. Figure 13.4 shows a Gaussian proposal around a current state and the acceptance probabilities of several proposals.

In our analogy, the explorer goes more often to densely populated neighborhoods. Suppose the explorer is in the Short North and the guidebook suggests visiting Upper Arlington. The explorer checks the population densities of both neighborhoods. If Upper Arlington is denser, the explorer goes there. If Upper Arlington has only 70% of the density of the Short North, the explorer goes there with a 70% chance. If the explorer decides not to go, they stay in the Short North for another day.

Checking Detailed Balance

We now verify that this acceptance probability satisfies detailed balance with respect to our target posterior distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\). Detailed balance requires that \[ p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = p(\mathbf{x}') T(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}). \]

Substituting the transition matrix gives \[ p(\mathbf{x}) q(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}) A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = p(\mathbf{x}') q(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{x}') A(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}). \]

The proposal distribution is symmetric, with \(q(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}) = q(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{x}')\). The condition therefore simplifies to \[ p(\mathbf{x}) A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = p(\mathbf{x}') A(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}). \]

We consider two cases. If \(p(\mathbf{x}') \geq p(\mathbf{x})\), then \[\begin{aligned} A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})}\right) = 1 \\ A(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')}\right) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')}. \end{aligned}\]

Substituting these into the detailed balance equation gives \[ p(\mathbf{x}) \cdot 1 = p(\mathbf{x}') \cdot \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')}, \] which simplifies to \(p(\mathbf{x}) = p(\mathbf{x})\) and is true.

If \(p(\mathbf{x}') < p(\mathbf{x})\), then \[\begin{aligned} A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})}\right) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})} \\ A(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')}\right) = 1. \end{aligned}\]

Substituting these into the detailed balance equation gives \[ p(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})} = p(\mathbf{x}') \cdot 1, \] which simplifies to \(p(\mathbf{x}') = p(\mathbf{x}')\) and is also true.

The transition matrix of the Metropolis algorithm therefore satisfies detailed balance with respect to our target posterior distribution. The posterior is thus a stationary distribution of the chain. Once the chain has converged to the target distribution, detailed balance keeps the flows between any two neighborhoods equal, so the equilibrium stays in place. If the chain has not yet converged, the net flows of people move the population distribution toward equilibrium. Neighborhoods with higher posterior probability gradually gain more residents, and neighborhoods with lower probability become less populated.

The Metropolis algorithm also has a practical advantage for Bayesian inference in astronomy. It requires only the ratio of posterior probabilities. We therefore avoid calculating the normalization constant, the Bayesian evidence, which is often intractable for complex models with many parameters. Written with the likelihood and the prior, the posterior ratio is \[ \frac{p(\mathbf{x}'|\mathcal{D})}{p(\mathbf{x}|\mathcal{D})} = \frac{p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{x}')p(\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathcal{D})}\frac{p(\mathcal{D})}{p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})} = \frac{p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{x}')p(\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})}. \]

The evidence \(p(\mathcal{D})\) cancels in the ratio. The remaining terms are the likelihood times the prior, which we can typically evaluate directly.

13.4 Convergence and Uniqueness in MCMC

Detailed balance shows only that the target posterior is one possible stationary distribution of the chain. It does not show that the chain converges. It also does not show that a converging chain ends at the correct distribution. In our Columbus analogy, a population that matches the true neighborhood densities is then a possible equilibrium. When we run MCMC in research, we need confidence that we will get the correct posterior. We therefore need two more properties, convergence and uniqueness.

Convergence means that the chain eventually settles into a pattern that matches our target posterior, whatever initial distribution we start with. We write this as \[ \lim_{n\to\infty} T^n \tilde{p}(\mathbf{x}) = p(\mathbf{x}), \] where \(\tilde{p}(\mathbf{x})\) is any starting distribution, \(T^n\) applies our transition matrix \(n\) times, and \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is our target distribution.

In the Columbus picture, we give the Metropolis guidebook to thousands of people who are spread over the city in various ways. Convergence means that, given enough time, they redistribute themselves over the neighborhoods to match the true population densities, wherever they started.

Uniqueness means that our chain has only one stationary distribution. Two stationary distributions \(p_1(\mathbf{x})\) and \(p_2(\mathbf{x})\) satisfy \[ (T p_1)(\mathbf{x}) = p_1(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{and} \quad (T p_2)(\mathbf{x}) = p_2(\mathbf{x}), \] and uniqueness requires that \(p_1(\mathbf{x}) = p_2(\mathbf{x})\). Detailed balance has shown that our target distribution is a stationary distribution. Uniqueness makes sure that it is the only one.

In the Columbus picture, the guidebook allows only one stable population spread over the neighborhoods. Without uniqueness, the population could settle into a distribution that does not match the true neighborhood densities, even after a very long run.

Two transition matrices fail to produce the sampling behavior we need for Bayesian inference, even though detailed balance holds. First, imagine a guidebook that simply says, “stay where you are.” Its transition matrix is \(T = \mathrm{Id}\), the identity matrix. This matrix satisfies detailed balance with respect to any distribution, because no one moves. If we start with everyone in the Short North, they all stay there, and a uniform population spread over Columbus stays uniform. The system “converges” at once, but the distribution it converges to depends on our starting point. This violates uniqueness, since we need the sampling process to converge to the correct posterior wherever we start.

For a second example, take a Columbus with only two neighborhoods, the Short North and German Village. The guidebook says, “If you are in the Short North today, go to German Village tomorrow. If you are in German Village today, go to the Short North tomorrow.” This guidebook has the transition matrix \[ T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

This transition matrix has the stationary distribution \(p^*(\mathbf{x}) = [0.5, 0.5]\). If half of the population starts in each neighborhood, the split stays at half and half as people swap back and forth. However, for any other starting distribution, the system does not converge. Instead, we get \[ p^{(t)}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \tilde{p}(\mathbf{x}), & \text{if } t \text{ is even} \\ 1 - \tilde{p}(\mathbf{x}), & \text{if } t \text{ is odd} .\end{cases} \]

Suppose we start with 70% of the people in the Short North and 30% in German Village. The next day the split flips to 30% in the Short North and 70% in German Village, and it keeps oscillating in this way.

These examples show two different failures. The identity matrix has many stationary distributions, so uniqueness fails. The swap matrix has one stationary distribution, but the chain does not converge to it from other starting distributions, so convergence fails. Most practical MCMC methods, including the Metropolis algorithm, have transition matrices built to avoid these pathological behaviors. These matrices satisfy an additional property called ergodicity, which guarantees both convergence and uniqueness.

13.5 Ergodicity Overview

The term ergodicity may be familiar from statistical mechanics, but the concept applies beyond physics. In essence, ergodicity means that a system can explore all its possible states over time and reach a stable equilibrium distribution. An ergodic Markov chain converges to a unique stationary distribution, whatever its starting point. A Markov chain is ergodic if it satisfies three properties.

The first property is irreducibility. The chain can go from any state to any other state in a finite number of steps. In our Columbus analogy, you can travel from any neighborhood to any other neighborhood given enough time. No area of the parameter space is isolated, so the chain cannot get trapped in one region and miss the rest of the posterior distribution. Figure 13.5 compares an irreducible chain with a reducible chain whose states form two groups that cannot reach each other.

The second property is aperiodicity. The chain does not visit states in a predictable cyclic pattern. This prevents the oscillation that we saw in our Short North and German Village example, where people swapped back and forth.

The third property is positive recurrence. A chain is recurrent when, from any state, it returns to that state with probability 1. It is positive recurrent when the expected time to return is also finite, which prevents the chain from wandering off to infinity.

In our Columbus analogy, travelers come back to a neighborhood they have visited within a finite expected time. They do not wander to suburbs farther and farther from the city center and take ever longer to return. Without positive recurrence, our population distribution would not settle into the desired equilibrium. In Figure 13.6, a walk on a bounded set of states keeps returning to its start, while a walk with drift moves away from it.

The three conditions together rule out the pathological cases that we met earlier. Irreducibility prevents the chain from getting stuck in isolated regions, like the “always stay where you are” example. Aperiodicity eliminates the cyclic oscillation of the Short North and German Village swapping. Positive recurrence stops the chain from drifting away, so that returns to previously visited areas take a finite expected time.

For a chain that satisfies all three conditions, we can prove two results. First, a unique stationary distribution exists. The chain has only one equilibrium distribution, so there is no ambiguity about the distribution we sample from. Second, the chain converges to this stationary distribution from any starting point. Wherever we initialize the chain, it reaches the same equilibrium distribution and stays there. A proof of convergence needs advanced probability theory, so the next sections give basic ideas and intuition before we return to applications and algorithms.

Convergence to a unique stationary distribution is what we need for MCMC to work correctly in our astronomical applications. It is analogous to gas particles in a closed room, which explore the available space until they reach equilibrium in a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Most MCMC methods used in astronomy, including the Metropolis algorithm, are built to satisfy the three conditions.

However, irreducibility can be violated if the posterior has separated modes with zero probability between them. This is like having two rooms with a vacuum between them, where particles that start in one room cannot reach the other. In astronomy, this can happen when a parameter space has several disconnected high-probability regions, separated by regions with nearly zero probability. Two equally valid solutions with no connecting path are an example. Widely separated modes can also leave the chain reducible in practice, so that it cannot explore the full posterior.

Aperiodicity is usually satisfied by default in standard MCMC implementations, unless we explicitly design a periodic transition scheme. The random acceptance or rejection step of the Metropolis algorithm typically gives aperiodicity. It does so through self-loops, which occur when a proposed move is rejected and the chain stays at the current state.

Positive recurrence is typically ensured when the priors limit the parameters to a finite range. This is like keeping particles in a finite room instead of an infinite universe, where they could wander without end. In astronomical models, this usually means choosing priors based on physically reasonable parameter ranges.

Astronomers often do not check for ergodicity explicitly in their MCMC runs. Knowing the three conditions still helps us diagnose problems when a method does not behave as expected. Suppose that multiple chains with different starting points fail to converge to the same distribution, although each chain looks fine on its own. This often indicates a violation of one of the conditions, most commonly irreducibility because of disconnected modes in the posterior.

13.6 The Uniqueness of the Stationary Distribution

The condition that guarantees uniqueness is irreducibility. We prove that an irreducible Markov chain has at most one stationary distribution.

An irreducible Markov chain can reach any state from any other state through a finite sequence of transitions. We define irreducibility as \[ \text{for all states } i, j \text{ there is a } t_{ij} \geq 0 \text{ such that } p(\mathbf{x}^{t_{ij}} = j | \mathbf{x}^0 = i) > 0. \] Here \(i\) and \(j\) are any two states, and \(\mathbf{x}^t\) is the state of the chain at step \(t\). The number \(t_{ij}\) is the number of steps needed to go from state \(i\) to state \(j\). The expression \(p(\mathbf{x}^{t_{ij}} = j | \mathbf{x}^0 = i)\) is the probability of being in state \(j\) after \(t_{ij}\) steps, given that we started in state \(i\).

The term irreducible comes from graph theory, where all nodes in the graph are connected. This connectivity allows us to prove uniqueness. We treat a finite state space. The result extends to general state spaces under appropriate technical conditions.

Since the chain is irreducible, there is an integer \(N\) such that the composite transition matrix \[ \tilde{T} \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{N} T^i \] has all strictly positive entries. Transitions over up to \(N\) steps therefore reach any state from any other state with positive probability.

Proof of Uniqueness

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that \(T\) has two distinct stationary distributions \(p\) and \(q\) (here \(q\) is not the proposal), with \(p \neq q\), so that \[ Tp = p, \quad Tq = q. \]

To see how \(\tilde{T}\) acts on \(p\), note that \(Tp = p\) gives \(T^2p = T(Tp) = Tp = p\) and, by induction, \(T^ip = p\) for any positive integer \(i\). Therefore \[ \tilde{T}p = \sum_{i=1}^{N} T^ip = \sum_{i=1}^{N} p = Np. \]

Since we work with probability distributions, we divide \(\tilde{T}\) by \(N\) and keep the name \(\tilde{T}\) for the normalized matrix. The same steps apply to \(q\). Both \(p\) and \(q\) are then stationary distributions of \(\tilde{T}\), so that \[ \tilde{T}p = p, \quad \tilde{T}q = q. \]

We write the first of these equations element by element as \[ p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}} \tilde{T}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) p(\mathbf{y}). \]

Let \(\mathbf{x}\) be the state that minimizes the ratio \(p(\mathbf{y})/q(\mathbf{y})\) over all states. This minimum exists because the state space is finite. We can then rewrite the equation for \(p(\mathbf{x})\) as \[ p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}} \tilde{T}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) q(\mathbf{y}) \frac{p(\mathbf{y})}{q(\mathbf{y})}. \]

Because \(\mathbf{x}\) minimizes the ratio \(p(\mathbf{y})/q(\mathbf{y})\), we know that \[ \frac{p(\mathbf{y})}{q(\mathbf{y})} \geq \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} \text{ for all } \mathbf{y}. \]

This gives us \[ p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}} \tilde{T}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) q(\mathbf{y}) \frac{p(\mathbf{y})}{q(\mathbf{y})} \geq \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} \sum_{\mathbf{y}} \tilde{T}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) q(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} q(\mathbf{x}) = p(\mathbf{x}). \]

The expression starts and ends with \(p(\mathbf{x})\), so the inequality is an equality, which means that \[ \frac{p(\mathbf{y})}{q(\mathbf{y})} = \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} \text{ for all } \mathbf{y} \text{ where } \tilde{T}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) > 0. \]

Because \(\tilde{T}\) has all positive entries, a consequence of irreducibility, this implies that \[ \frac{p(\mathbf{y})}{q(\mathbf{y})} = \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} \text{ for all } \mathbf{y}. \]

The ratio of the two distributions is therefore the same for all states. Both \(p\) and \(q\) are probability distributions, which means that \[ \sum_{\mathbf{y}} p(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}} q(\mathbf{y}) = 1. \]

A constant ratio and equal sums leave only one possibility, \(p(\mathbf{y}) = q(\mathbf{y})\) for all \(\mathbf{y}\). This contradicts our assumption that \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct. Hence an irreducible Markov chain with a finite number of states has only one stationary distribution.

We can also understand this result through linear algebra. The Perron-Frobenius theorem says that an irreducible non-negative matrix, such as our transition matrix, has a largest real eigenvalue that occurs only once. For a transition matrix this eigenvalue equals 1. Its right eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) is a column with \(T\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\), its left eigenvector \(\mathbf{u}\) is a row with \(\mathbf{u}T = \mathbf{u}\), and both are positive. Our definition of stationarity sums \(p(\mathbf{x}) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\) over \(\mathbf{x}\), which multiplies \(T\) from the left, so it involves the left eigenvector. We normalize the left eigenvector so that it sums to 1, and it is then the stationary distribution of the Markov chain.

13.7 Convergence to the Stationary Distribution

Irreducibility gives at most one stationary distribution. We now ask whether the chain converges to it from any starting point. Uniqueness alone does not guarantee this, and we need additional conditions. To see why, we revisit the oscillating example.

The transition matrix of this example is \[ T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Period and Aperiodicity

This chain has the stationary distribution \(p^*(\mathbf{x}) = [0.5, 0.5]\), but it converges to this distribution only if we start with it. If everyone starts in state 1, the population moves to state 2 on the next step, then back to state 1, and so on. The chain is periodic, since a state can be revisited only at regular intervals. Aperiodicity is our second condition for convergence.

We define the period \(k_i\) of a state \(i\) as the greatest common divisor (gcd) of all possible return times \[ k_i = \text{gcd}\{t : p(z^{(t)} = i | z^{(0)} = i) > 0\}. \] Here \(z^{(t)}\) is the state of the chain at step \(t\). The expression \(p(z^{(t)} = i | z^{(0)} = i)\) is the probability of returning to state \(i\) after \(t\) steps, given that we started at state \(i\). The gcd is the largest integer that divides all of these return times.

In the oscillating example, a traveler who starts in state 1 can return only after an even number of steps. This follows from \[\begin{aligned} p(z^{(1)} = 1 | z^{(0)} = 1) &= 0 \\ p(z^{(2)} = 1 | z^{(0)} = 1) &> 0 \\ p(z^{(3)} = 1 | z^{(0)} = 1) &= 0 \\ p(z^{(4)} = 1 | z^{(0)} = 1) &> 0. \end{aligned}\] The return times are 2, 4, 6, ..., so the gcd is 2 and the period is \(k = 2\).

A Markov chain is aperiodic if all states have period 1, that is, if the possible return times have no common divisor larger than 1. In a chain with period \(k > 1\), the distribution after a large number of steps \(n\) depends on the remainder of \(n\) divided by \(k\). The chain then cycles through \(k\) different distributions instead of settling into a single stationary distribution. In an aperiodic chain, this cycling disappears. The distribution depends less and less on the exact number of steps and can settle into the stationary distribution.

One way to make a chain aperiodic is to allow self-loops, which are transitions from a state back to itself. In our Columbus analogy, travelers would have the option to stay in their current neighborhood with some non-zero probability. Even a single self-loop in a chain can break periodicity, which helps convergence. A state with a self-loop can be revisited after 1 step, 2 steps, 3 steps, and so on. The gcd of the set \(\{1,2,3,...\}\) is 1, so the state is aperiodic. Figure 13.7 shows a chain with period 3 and the same chain after we add a self-loop to state 2.

The Metropolis algorithm produces self-loops because we may reject a proposed move. We reject a proposal with probability \(1-A\), and the chain then remains at the current state \(\mathbf{x}\). This self-loop means that the Metropolis algorithm typically satisfies the aperiodicity condition.

Positive Recurrence

Irreducibility and aperiodicity together do not guarantee that a stationary distribution exists, or that the chain converges to it. To see this, consider a simple random walk on the integers with the transition probabilities \[ T_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1/3, & j \in \{i-1, i, i+1\} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} .\end{cases} \]

This chain is irreducible, since we can reach any integer from any other integer by moving one position at a time. It is also aperiodic because of its self-loops. From any state \(i\) we can return to \(i\) in 1 step (with probability \(1/3\)), in 2 steps, in 3 steps, and so on. The gcd of these return times is 1.

Does this chain have a stationary distribution? Suppose that \(\pi = (\pi_0, \pi_1, \pi_2, ...)\) is the stationary distribution, where \(\pi_i\) is the probability of being in state \(i\) after a long run. By definition \[ \pi_i = \frac{1}{3}\pi_{i-1} + \frac{1}{3}\pi_i + \frac{1}{3}\pi_{i+1}. \]

Rearranging gives \[ \pi_{i-1} - 2\pi_i + \pi_{i+1} = 0. \]

This is a second-order linear recurrence relation, which gives \(\pi_{i+1} = 2\pi_i - \pi_{i-1}\). Working out the first terms, we find \(\pi_2 = 2\pi_1 - \pi_0\), \(\pi_3 = 3\pi_1 - 2\pi_0\) and \(\pi_4 = 4\pi_1 - 3\pi_0\). The pattern gives the general solution \[ \pi_i = i\pi_1 - (i-1)\pi_0. \]

We now check whether this solution can be a probability distribution. If \(\pi_1 = \pi_0 > 0\), then \(\pi_i = \pi_0\) for all \(i\), a uniform distribution over infinitely many states with \(\sum_i \pi_i = \infty\) instead of 1. If \(\pi_1 = \pi_0 = 0\), then \(\pi_i = 0\) for all \(i\) and \(\sum_i \pi_i = 0\), which also violates the normalization. If \(\pi_1 > \pi_0\), then \(\pi_i\) grows linearly with \(i\) and \(\sum_i \pi_i = \infty\). If \(\pi_1 < \pi_0\), then \(\pi_i\) eventually becomes negative for large \(i\), which violates the requirement that probabilities are non-negative.

This contradiction shows that the random walk has no valid stationary distribution. The issue is that the chain can move away to infinity.

Unlike Columbus, which has a finite number of neighborhoods, this random walk moves through an unbounded space. It has no “gravitational force” that pulls the population toward a central region. At each step, a traveler moves left, stays put or moves right, each with probability \(1/3\). As time progresses, the population disperses more and more widely over the infinite state space, with no stable configuration. The probability mass spreads thinner and thinner as an expanding frontier of states fills up.

The random walk shows why we need a third condition, positive recurrence, to guarantee convergence. With positive recurrence, the chain has a well-defined stationary distribution and does not escape to infinity. A state \(i\) is positive recurrent if its expected return time, starting from \(i\), is finite, which means that \[ \mathbb{E}[t_i] < \infty, \text{ where } t_i = \inf\{t \geq 1 : z^{(t)} = i | z^{(0)} = i\}. \]Here \(t_i\) is the return time, the number of steps until the chain first comes back to state \(i\). The notation \(\inf\) means the smallest value, here the smallest \(t \geq 1\) with \(z^{(t)} = i\) when the chain starts in state \(i\).

In the Columbus picture, a traveler who starts in any neighborhood returns to that neighborhood in a finite expected time. The random walk on the integers is recurrent, since a traveler returns to each state with probability 1. Yet any state has an infinite expected return time, because a traveler can wander arbitrarily far away before returning. This is why the chain fails to converge, although it is irreducible and aperiodic.

Ergodic Chains

The combination of irreducibility, aperiodicity and positive recurrence defines an ergodic Markov chain. For ergodic chains we can prove several results. First, the long-run fraction of time spent in each state converges to a unique stationary distribution, whatever the starting state. Second, the stationary probability of a state is the inverse of its expected return time, \(p^*(i) = 1/\mathbb{E}[t_i]\). Third, for any initial distribution \(\tilde{p}(\mathbf{x})\), repeated application of the transition operator converges to the unique stationary distribution, \(\lim_{n \to \infty} T^n \tilde{p}(\mathbf{x}) = p^*(\mathbf{x})\).

A traveler walks through the state space for a long time. The footprints that mark each visited location trace out a density map proportional to the stationary distribution, with denser clusters at more frequently visited states. With the target posterior as the stationary distribution, we can generate samples from complex distributions by running the chain and recording its states.

13.8 Implementing Metropolis Algorithm

The acceptance probability of the Metropolis algorithm ensures detailed balance for our target distribution. Ergodicity, which we typically have in practice, then makes the chain converge to this target. The algorithm has the following steps.

  1. Initialize. Choose a starting point \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\) in the parameter space.

  2. For each iteration \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, N\), where \(N\) is the number of iterations.

    1. Propose. Generate a proposed state \(\mathbf{x}'\) from a symmetric proposal distribution centered at the current state, \(\mathbf{x}' \sim q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)})\), where \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) = q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')\).

    2. Compute. Calculate the acceptance probability \(A(\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}, \mathbf{x}') = \min(1, p(\mathbf{x}')/p(\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}))\).

    3. Accept or reject. Draw a uniform random number \(u \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)\). If \(u \leq A(\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}, \mathbf{x}')\), accept the proposal and set \(\mathbf{x}^{(t)} = \mathbf{x}'\). Otherwise, reject it and stay at the current position, \(\mathbf{x}^{(t)} = \mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}\).

  3. Return. The sequence \(\{\mathbf{x}^{(0)}, \mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(N)}\}\) forms the samples from the target distribution. Every iteration adds an entry to this sequence. If we reject the proposal, the entry repeats the current state. We typically discard an initial portion as burn-in, which we explain below.

Figure 13.8 shows the starting state and the steps Propose, Compute and Accept or reject on a multimodal distribution.

Each state of a Markov chain depends only on the preceding state and not on the earlier history. This property leads to two practical questions. First, how do we handle the early samples, taken before the chain has reached its stationary distribution (the target posterior)? Second, once the chain has converged, how do we account for the correlation between consecutive samples, which reduces their statistical efficiency?

The first question concerns burn-in, the warm-up period of the chain. The chain starts from an arbitrary position \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\) that may be far from the high-probability regions of the distribution. The initial samples then depend on this starting position and do not represent the target distribution. The chain converges to the target distribution in the end, but this takes time.

Imagine that our explorer starts from the outskirts of an unfamiliar city. The first movements go into finding the city center, and only then can the explorer begin to explore the important areas. The chain likewise needs time to find the high-probability regions. Figure 13.9 shows a chain that starts in a low-probability region and settles into the high-probability regions after the burn-in. We cannot compare the chain with the target in practice, so the burn-in section below shows how to find its end and shorten it.

The second question concerns the efficiency of the sampler. Given enough time, MCMC can in theory sample any distribution, but even when ergodicity holds the time to convergence can be prohibitively long. Astronomical research has limited computing resources and project timelines. The question therefore shifts from “Can we sample this distribution?” to “How efficiently can we sample it?”

13.9 Proposal Mechanisms and Sampling Efficiency

The efficiency of an MCMC method depends on how well the chain covers the parameter space. We control this exploration through the mechanism that proposes new positions for the chain to visit. This mechanism differs between MCMC algorithms but follows similar principles. Sequential steps turn difficult sampling tasks into manageable random walks, so MCMC can handle complex, high-dimensional problems. However, this same property requires us to choose with care how the random walk moves.

In most MCMC algorithms, a transition consists of a proposal followed by an acceptance or rejection step. The details differ between the Metropolis algorithm above and the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and Gibbs sampling, which we introduce later. All of them must balance local exploration against global coverage of the parameter space.

For a symmetric proposal distribution, the Metropolis transition probability is \[ T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}'), \] where \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})\) is the proposal distribution and \(A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\) is the acceptance probability. The choice of proposal mechanism affects how efficiently we sample from the posterior, in any MCMC variant.

In astronomy, a common proposal is a multivariate Gaussian, \[ q(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}), \] where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the covariance matrix that sets the scale and orientation of the proposals. The choice of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) directly affects the sampling efficiency.

In practice, any MCMC method must balance small moves against large moves. Small moves are likely to be accepted but explore slowly. Large moves explore faster but are more likely to be rejected. This balance affects how quickly the chain converges to the target distribution and how efficiently it samples once converged.

If the proposal mechanism is too conservative, the chain has a high acceptance rate but moves through the parameter space very slowly. In our Columbus analogy, we take tiny steps. We accept nearly all of them because we stay close to where we are, but exploring the city takes an impractically long time. If the proposal mechanism is too aggressive, most proposals land in low-probability regions and are rejected. We then attempt giant leaps across the city, but most of them land in unlikely areas, so we often remain in the same location. Figure 13.10 compares a narrow and a wide proposal distribution.

Acceptance Rate and Tuning

The acceptance rate is the proportion of proposed moves that the chain accepts during sampling. It is a simple diagnostic of the efficiency of many MCMC algorithms. It gives a first idea of how well the chain moves through the parameter space.

A proposal mechanism that is too conservative gives a very high acceptance rate. This may look desirable, but it leads to inefficient sampling. The chain moves through the parameter space in tiny steps, so the samples are highly correlated. We accept nearly all steps, but we cover little ground and gather largely redundant information. The chain needs many iterations to explore the full posterior distribution, so we say that it mixes poorly. A chain mixes well when it moves quickly through the region of high posterior probability, so that its samples soon look independent.

A proposal mechanism that is too aggressive gives a very low acceptance rate. Most proposals jump to regions with much lower posterior probability and are rejected. The chain stays at the same position for many iterations, which again gives highly correlated samples. This resembles exploring a city by teleporting across vast distances. Most attempts land in unlikely places, so we stand still most of the time.

The best case typically occurs when the proposal mechanism is tuned to the geometry of the posterior distribution. For random walk proposals like the Gaussian proposal above, acceptance rates around 20 to 40% tend to give the most efficient sampling. At these rates the moves are large enough to explore the parameter space effectively, but not so large that nearly all proposals are rejected.

In astronomy, models are complex and computing resources are limited. Proper tuning of the proposal mechanism can mean that reliable posterior inferences take hours instead of days. Finding the best tuning often takes some experimentation. We can start with an educated guess based on prior knowledge of the problem. We then adjust it based on the acceptance rate in a short pilot run.

The shape of the proposal matters as much as its size. A round Gaussian proposal wastes steps when the parameters have different scales or are correlated. A better choice sets \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) proportional to the covariance of the posterior, so that the steps match its scales and correlations. We estimate this covariance from the samples of the pilot run. We then adjust its overall scale with the acceptance rate, as above.

Acceptance rates are a useful rule of thumb for this initial tuning, but they do not fully describe the sampling efficiency. To see how well the chain covers the parameter space and how much independent information we obtain, we need the correlation between successive samples.

13.10 Autocorrelation in MCMC Sampling

Successive samples of an MCMC chain are not independent, because each new state depends on the previous one. This correlation is called autocorrelation. It reduces the effective information content of the chain compared to independent samples, and we need to measure it for reliable statistical inference. For \(N\) independent and identically distributed samples, the standard error of our estimate decreases as \(1/\sqrt{N}\). Correlated samples give a larger error for the same \(N\). Each new correlated sample carries less new information about the target distribution than an independent sample, so the estimates are less precise.

The autocorrelation at lag \(k\) of \(\{X_0, X_1, X_2, ...\}\) is defined as \[ R(k) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X_t - \mu)(X_{t+k} - \mu)]}{\sigma^2}, \] where \(\mu = \mathbb{E}[X_t]\) and \(\sigma^2 = \mathbb{E}[(X_t - \mu)^2]\) are the mean and variance of the stationary distribution. This definition follows the correlation coefficient of Chapter 3. Standard correlation measures the linear relationship between two different variables. Autocorrelation measures the relationship between observations of the same variable at different points in the sequence. The lag \(k\) is the number of steps between these points.

In a Markov chain, we can view \(X_t\) and \(X_{t+k}\) as two realizations of the same random variable. Once the chain has reached its stationary distribution, each state it visits is a draw from that distribution. Both \(X_t\) and \(X_{t+k}\) approximately follow the target distribution, and the evolution of the chain over \(k\) steps connects them.

This view rests on the ergodic properties of a well-designed MCMC algorithm. For an ergodic chain, the average over time along the chain, the time average, becomes equivalent to the ensemble average. The ensemble average is the average over many independent samples from the target distribution. This equivalence lets us use a single chain to characterize a probability distribution.

The dependency between samples is the trade-off we accept for sampling complex distributions through random walks. The results are still correct in the long run, but the sampling noise is larger than for independent samples. We need to understand this correlation to judge the uncertainty of our estimates and to choose the chain length. Figure 13.11 shows a chain and how the correlation between its values at steps \(t\) and \(t+k\) decreases as the lag \(k\) grows. Once the lag is large enough, points of the chain are approximately independent samples of the target distribution. This holds for a chain that mixes well.

In practice, we estimate the autocorrelation from the finite chain. For a chain of length \(N\), the autocorrelation at lag \(k\) is estimated by \[ r(k) = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{N-k} (X_t - \bar{X})(X_{t+k} - \bar{X})}{\sum_{t=1}^{N} (X_t - \bar{X})^2}, \] where \(\bar{X}\) is the sample mean of the chain. This estimator replaces the mean and variance of the definition by sample values. The numerator is the covariance of samples separated by lag \(k\), and the denominator normalizes it by the sample variance. Only \(N-k\) pairs of points are available at lag \(k\), and their number falls as \(k\) increases. The estimate therefore becomes less reliable at high lags.

To build intuition for autocorrelation, we look at different proposal mechanisms. When the proposal distribution is too conservative (too narrow), each new sample is very close to the previous one. The chain moves like a cautious explorer taking baby steps and stays near the same location for many iterations. The value at position \(t\) then predicts the values at positions \(t+1\), \(t+2\) and so on, which gives high autocorrelation even at large lags. We have many samples, but they hold the same information repeated with slight variations.

When the proposal distribution is too aggressive (too wide), most proposals are rejected because they jump to low-probability regions. The chain stays at the same value for many iterations, which creates high autocorrelation through a different mechanism, the literal repetition of the same value. When jumps do occur they can be substantial, but they are too infrequent for good exploration. A well-tuned proposal moves enough to explore effectively and keeps a reasonable acceptance rate. The autocorrelation then typically decays more rapidly with the lag, which means that each new sample brings more unique information about the target distribution. This is the balance we aim for when we tune an MCMC algorithm for efficient sampling.

The autocorrelation function shows how efficient the sampler is. Independent samples have no relationship with each other, so knowing one value tells us nothing about another and \(R(k) = 0\) for \(k > 0\). In MCMC, we typically observe an autocorrelation that decays as the lag increases. The rate of this decay sets how efficiently the chain covers the parameter space. A rapidly decaying autocorrelation means that the chain quickly “forgets” its starting position and samples the distribution more independently. A faster decay is desirable, because it leads to more efficient parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification.

13.11 Effective Sample Size

To measure the loss of information caused by autocorrelation, we use the effective sample size (ESS) that we met for importance sampling in Chapter 12. The ESS is the number of independent samples that would carry the same amount of information as our autocorrelated chain. More samples do not necessarily mean more useful information if the samples are highly correlated.

Imagine an explorer mapping the population distribution of Columbus. A path with high autocorrelation revisits the same neighborhoods for many days or follows predictable patterns. This gives a poor picture of the population distribution of the city, even after a long exploration. A path with low autocorrelation moves through the city in varied, seemingly random ways and gives a more representative view in less time. In MCMC terms, lower autocorrelation means more efficient sampling of the target distribution and a larger effective sample size.

Deriving the Effective Sample Size

We derive the ESS from the variance of the sample mean of a correlated chain.

The sample mean of our MCMC chain is \[ \bar{X} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i. \]

The variance of this estimator is \[ \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \text{Var}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i\right) = \frac{1}{N^2}\text{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i\right). \]

For our MCMC chain, we must account for all pairwise relationships between samples. Expanding the variance of the sum gives \[ \text{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j). \]

The covariance between two samples of a stationary Markov chain depends only on the lag between them. We call a chain stationary once it has reached its stationary distribution, because its statistical properties then no longer change from step to step. Once the chain has converged, we have \[ \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = \text{Cov}(X_1, X_{1+|i-j|}) = \sigma^2 R(|i-j|), \] where \(|i-j|\) is the lag between the samples and \(\sigma^2\) is the variance of each sample. The function \(R(k)\) is the autocorrelation at lag \(k\). Note that \(R(0) = 1\), because a sample correlates with itself.

We reorganize the double sum by grouping all pairs that have the same lag. For example, the pairs \((1,3)\), \((2,4)\) and \((3,5)\) all have a lag of 2. For a chain of length \(N\), there are \(N-k\) pairs with lag \(k\). With this count, we can rewrite the variance as \[ \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{N^2}\left[N + 2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)R(k)\right]. \]

The first term \(N\) counts the pairs with lag 0 (that is, \(i=j\)), where \(R(0)=1\). The factor of 2 in the sum appears because we count both the pairs \((i,i+k)\) and \((i+k,i)\) for each positive lag \(k\). These pairs have the same autocorrelation due to stationarity.

We divide the numerator and the denominator by \(N\) and simplify further to \[ \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{N}\left[1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{N}\right)R(k)\right]. \]

For large \(N\), the term \(k/N\) becomes negligible for any fixed lag \(k\), so we can approximate \[ \text{Var}(\bar{X}) \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{N}\left(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}R(k)\right). \]

This result shows that the variance of our sample mean is inflated by the factor \(\left(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}R(k)\right)\) compared to independent samples. This inflation factor measures the information loss caused by autocorrelation in our chain.

The mean of ESS independent samples has the variance \(\sigma^2/\text{ESS}\), which we equate with our MCMC variance \[ \frac{\sigma^2}{\text{ESS}} = \frac{\sigma^2}{N}\left(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}R(k)\right). \]

Solving for the ESS gives \[ \text{ESS} = \frac{N}{1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}R(k)}. \]

The denominator \(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}R(k)\) is the autocorrelation time \(\tau\), the average number of correlated MCMC samples needed to obtain the equivalent of one independent sample. If our samples were independent, as in direct sampling methods, all autocorrelations \(R(k)\) would be zero for \(k > 0\). The denominator would then equal 1 and \(\text{ESS} = N\), which means that all our samples carry full information. When samples are highly correlated, as is typical in MCMC, the autocorrelations \(R(k)\) remain positive for many lags. The sum in the denominator is then large, so the denominator exceeds 1 and the ESS falls below \(N\). The stronger and more persistent these autocorrelations are, the smaller the ESS becomes relative to \(N\).

For example, if the autocorrelation time equals 20, we need about 20 MCMC samples to get the information of one independent sample. A chain of 10,000 samples then has an ESS of only about 500, so our precision equals that of 500 independent samples. This is why tuning the proposal distribution is so important. A well-tuned proposal reduces autocorrelation and increases the ESS for a given computational budget.

As a rule of thumb, we aim for ESS \(> 100\) for reliable posterior estimates. More demanding applications may need higher values. An ESS of this size gives enough independent information to estimate posterior means and standard deviations.

Calculating the autocorrelation function \(R(k)\) directly takes \(O(N^2)\) operations, which is slow for long chains. The fast Fourier transform gives a much faster method. The power spectrum of the chain is the squared magnitude of its Fourier transform. It shows how much of the variation of the chain sits at each frequency. The Wiener-Khinchin theorem says that the autocorrelation function is the inverse Fourier transform of the power spectrum. The cost then falls to \(O(N \log N)\), which is practical for the long chains typical of astronomical applications.

13.12 Thinning MCMC Chains

Given the autocorrelation in MCMC samples, a common practice is “thinning”, which keeps only every \(m\)-th sample of the chain to reduce correlation. For example, from a chain of 10,000 samples we might keep every 10th sample, which gives a thinned chain of 1,000 samples. If successive samples are highly correlated, keeping every sample may give redundant information. Thinning also reduces the storage and computation needed for the later analysis.

Thinning can be beneficial in several contexts. When storing or processing samples is costly, thinning reduces this cost while keeping a representative sample of the posterior. When the autocorrelation is very strong, thinning makes the data more manageable for analysis and visualization. Certain Monte Carlo estimators also perform better with less correlated samples, which makes thinning advantageous in those applications. However, thinning discards some information, because even correlated samples contain some independent information about the target distribution. For posterior means and credible intervals, the full chain after burn-in generally gives more precise estimates than a thinned chain of the same computing cost.

We can compare the variance of estimators computed from thinned and from full chains. Consider a chain of length \(N\) with autocorrelation function \(R(k)\). If we thin by keeping every \(m\)-th sample, we obtain a chain of length \(N/m\) with a modified autocorrelation structure. Samples separated by lag \(k\) in the thinned chain are separated by lag \(mk\) in the original chain. The thinned chain therefore has the autocorrelation function \(R_{\text{thin}}(k) = R(mk)\).

The effective sample size of the thinned chain is \[ \text{ESS}_{\text{thin}} = \frac{N/m}{1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}R(mk)}. \]

Comparing this to the ESS of the full chain shows the trade-off of thinning. Thinning reduces the autocorrelation between consecutive samples in the thinned chain, but it also reduces the total number of samples. The net effect on the statistical efficiency depends on the autocorrelation structure of the original chain.

To understand when thinning might be beneficial, consider two extreme cases. If the original chain has very weak autocorrelation, the samples are nearly independent. Then \(R(k) \approx 0\) for \(k > 0\) and the ESS of the full chain is about \(N\). Thinning this chain by a factor \(m\) gives an ESS of about \(N/m\), which is worse than using the full chain. If instead the original chain has very strong autocorrelation that persists for many lags, thinning might remove redundant information without reducing the ESS much. The thinned chain might then keep most of the information of the full chain and be much more manageable computationally.

The decision to thin should therefore balance computational constraints against statistical precision. In many astronomical applications, we are mainly interested in posterior summaries and uncertainties. We should then apply thinning with care and not as a default practice.

The balance between storage costs and statistical efficiency matters most in astronomical applications where chains may contain millions of samples across hundreds of parameters. In such cases, thinning saves computing time and storage. These savings may outweigh the loss of statistical precision, especially if the original chain has very high autocorrelation. However, modern computing resources and efficient storage formats often make it feasible to work with full chains. Thinning is therefore less necessary than in earlier decades of MCMC applications. We resort to thinning only when computational constraints make it necessary or when the autocorrelation structure suggests that little information would be lost.

A practical approach bases the thinning factor on the lag \(k_0\) at which the autocorrelation function drops to negligible values, say below 0.1. Thinning by a factor of \(k_0\) then keeps samples that are approximately independent. Figure 13.12 shows this choice of the thinning factor for chains with three proposal widths.

13.13 Burn-in

The discussion of autocorrelation and effective sample size assumed that the chain had already converged to its stationary distribution, the target posterior. Samples taken before convergence would bias the posterior estimates and lead to incorrect inferences. We therefore need to know when the burn-in is over, that is, when the chain has converged enough to start collecting useful samples.

In our Columbus analogy, observations that the explorer makes during the burn-in would skew the picture of the demographics of Columbus. We cannot compare the chain with samples of the target distribution, which is why we use MCMC in the first place. We therefore rely on diagnostics that examine the behavior of the chain itself to tell when burn-in has completed.

The simplest and most common approach is visual inspection of trace plots, which show the parameter values at each iteration of the chain. A well-converged chain should settle around a central value, fluctuating around a stable mean without obvious drift or trends. The width of the fluctuations stays roughly constant. The chain does not get stuck at particular values for extended periods, because such “stickiness” indicates poor mixing. It also covers the posterior properly, visiting all relevant regions of the parameter space with frequencies proportional to their posterior probabilities.

Beyond visual inspection, the ESS that we discussed earlier is another convergence diagnostic. The ESS depends on the autocorrelation structure of the chain, so monitoring how it changes as we include more samples gives insight into convergence. For a well-converged chain, the ESS should grow approximately linearly with the number of samples after burn-in. Plotted against the number of iterations, it should show an initial nonlinear phase during burn-in and a roughly linear increase once the chain has converged. A low ESS relative to the chain length may indicate poor mixing and convergence issues. A high ESS does not guarantee convergence, because a chain can mix well in one region without fully exploring the target.

Visual inspection and ESS calculations provide useful initial diagnostics. They become impractical for complex models with many parameters and may miss subtle convergence problems. We then need quantitative diagnostics that detect when chains have reached their target distributions. The Gelman-Rubin and Geweke diagnostics are two standard examples.

13.13.1 Gelman-Rubin Diagnostic

Convergence can be checked by running multiple chains from different starting points and comparing their behavior. The starting points should be dispersed over the parameter space. If all chains converge to the same distribution, they should be statistically indistinguishable from each other after some burn-in period. The Gelman-Rubin diagnostic formalizes this intuition. For a parameter \(x\), we run \(M\) chains, typically at least 3 or 4, each of length \(2N\). We consider discarding the first \(N\) iterations of each chain as burn-in and compare the within-chain variance with the between-chain variance.

Let \(x_{ij}\) be the \(i\)-th sample of parameter \(x\) in the \(j\)-th chain after the burn-in. For each chain \(j\), the mean \(\bar{x}_j\) is \[ \bar{x}_j = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{ij}, \] and the variance \(s_j^2\) is \[ s_j^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2. \]

The within-chain variance \(W\) is the average of these individual variances \[ W = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}s_j^2. \] If the chains have converged, \(W\) should directly estimate the variance \(\sigma^2\) of the target distribution.

For the between-chain variance, we first take the variance of the chain means \[ \text{Var}(\bar{x}_j) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}(\bar{x}_j - \bar{x})^2, \] where \(\bar{x} = (1/M)\sum_{j=1}^{M}\bar{x}_j\) is the overall mean over all chains.

The variance of the chain means is not directly comparable to \(W\). Each mean \(\bar{x}_j\) is based on \(N\) samples. Statistical theory gives \(\text{Var}(\bar{x}_j) = \sigma^2/N\) when the chain has converged to the target distribution. This is \(N\) times smaller than the variance of individual samples.

To make the between-chain variance comparable to the within-chain variance, we define \(B\) by multiplying by \(N\) \[ B = N \cdot \text{Var}(\bar{x}_j) = \frac{N}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}(\bar{x}_j - \bar{x})^2. \]

For converged chains, \(\text{Var}(\bar{x}_j) = \sigma^2/N\) gives \(B = N \cdot \sigma^2/N = \sigma^2\). The within-chain variance \(W\) also estimates \(\sigma^2\), so we expect \[ B \approx W. \]

Chains that have not converged explore different regions of the parameter space. Their means then differ by much more than for converged chains, so \(B\) is much larger than \(W\). This extra spread indicates additional uncertainty due to incomplete convergence.

The Gelman-Rubin statistic \(\hat{R}\) compares \(B\) and \(W\) through \[ \hat{R} = \sqrt{1 + \frac{B-W}{NW}}. \]

The expression under the square root is the ratio of \(W + (B-W)/N\) to \(W\). The numerator is our estimate of the marginal posterior variance, which includes both the within-chain and the between-chain variability. Its second term \((B-W)/N\) is the additional variance due to the variability between the chains. Dividing by \(W\) compares this total variance with the within-chain variance alone. The ratio has no units, so \(\hat{R}\) can be interpreted in the same way for parameters of different scales.

As the chains converge, \(\hat{R}\) approaches 1 from above, because the excess \(B-W\) is divided by \(N\). Values substantially greater than 1 indicate that the chains have not yet converged. The criterion typically used is \(\hat{R} < 1.1\) for acceptable convergence, or \(\hat{R} < 1.05\) for a more stringent requirement. These thresholds are practical compromises between computing cost and accuracy. The value \(\hat{R} = 1\) is rarely reached with finite samples. Figure 13.13 shows \(B\), \(W\) and \(\hat{R}\) for four chains that start from widely separated points.

To see the diagnostic intuitively, think of \(M\) explorers who start from different parts of Columbus. If they have all learned the true population distribution of the city, they should report similar statistics about the neighborhood populations. This means a low between-explorer variance. If their reports differ widely, this suggests that they have not fully explored the city or are still affected by their starting locations.

The diagnostic does not use the target distribution. It only compares the behavior of different chains. It does require several chains, which increases the computing cost.

The statistic \(\hat{R}\) measures the factor by which credible intervals might shrink with more sampling. For example, \(\hat{R} = 1.2\) suggests that credible intervals from the current chains might be about 20% wider than after full convergence.

In multivariate problems, we apply the diagnostic to each parameter separately. This shows which parameters may have convergence issues. However, the diagnostic may miss problems in parameters that we do not check. It also cannot detect complex interactions between parameters that indicate convergence problems even when each parameter looks well-behaved.

13.13.2 Geweke Diagnostic

The Gelman-Rubin diagnostic needs multiple chains. Limited computational resources or other practical constraints can rule this out. In such cases, we can use the Geweke diagnostic, which tests convergence with a single MCMC chain. If a chain has converged to its stationary distribution, different segments of the chain should have similar statistical properties. In particular, the means of different portions should be approximately equal, because all portions sample from the same target distribution.

To implement the Geweke diagnostic, we first run a single chain and discard the initial burn-in period. We then compare two segments of the remaining \(N\) samples, segment \(A\) and segment \(B\). Segment \(A\) holds the first \(N_A\) samples, typically the first 10% of the post-burn-in chain, and has mean \(\bar{x}_A\). Segment \(B\) holds the last \(N_B\) samples, typically the last 50% of the post-burn-in chain, and has mean \(\bar{x}_B\). These proportions give each segment enough samples for a reliable estimate. They also keep the two segments far enough apart in the chain to detect remaining non-convergence.

The two means are \[ \bar{x}_A = \frac{1}{N_A}\sum_{i=1}^{N_A}x_i, \] and \[ \bar{x}_B = \frac{1}{N_B}\sum_{i=N-N_B+1}^{N}x_i. \]

Accounting for Autocorrelation

If the chain has converged, the two means should be equal except for random sampling variation. To judge whether an observed difference exceeds this variation, we need the uncertainty of our estimates of the means. However, the samples of the chain are not independent. As the sections on autocorrelation and effective sample size show, consecutive samples are correlated, and this affects the standard error of the sample mean. The standard formula for independent samples would underestimate the true uncertainty and make our test too sensitive.

We therefore need the variance of the sample mean of an autocorrelated chain. We saw earlier that autocorrelation inflates it by a factor that depends on the autocorrelation function, so that \[ \text{Var}(\bar{x}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{N}\left(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}R(k)\right) \equiv S. \]The symbol \(S\) denotes this variance of the sample mean, which includes the effect of the autocorrelation at all lags.

A chain has finite length, so we cannot sum an infinite number of autocorrelation terms. Estimates of the autocorrelation at high lags are also increasingly noisy, because fewer pairs of observations are available. We therefore use a windowed estimator \[ \hat{S} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{N}\left(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{l} w(k, l) r(k)\right), \] where \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) is the sample variance of the segment and \(r(k)\) the estimated autocorrelation. Here \(N\) is the length of the segment, so \(N = N_A\) for \(\hat{S}_A\) and \(N = N_B\) for \(\hat{S}_B\). The window function \(w(k, l)\) does not increase with \(k\), for example \(1 - k/l\), and \(l\) is the maximum lag. The term \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) estimates the marginal variance of the target distribution from the available samples, while the remaining terms adjust for the autocorrelation structure.

The windowed estimator can be viewed as integrating over a triangular region in lag space. For the window \(1 - k/l\), the weight decreases linearly with \(k\) and is zero beyond lag \(l\). Small lags receive the largest weight, because they matter more and are more reliable in describing the autocorrelation structure of the chain.

With the estimates \(\hat{S}_A\) and \(\hat{S}_B\) of this variance for the two segments, the Geweke statistic is the Z-score \[ Z = \frac{\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B}{\sqrt{\hat{S}_A + \hat{S}_B}}. \]

The Z-score is the difference between the means, divided by the standard error of that difference, which is adjusted for autocorrelation. Under the null hypothesis that the chain has converged, meaning that both segments sample the same distribution, \(Z\) should approximately follow a standard normal distribution. This follows from the Central Limit Theorem for Markov chains, which says that the mean of a long chain is approximately normal. In practice, we typically consider the chain converged if \(|Z| < 2\), which contains about 95% of the standard normal distribution. Larger Z-scores suggest that the chain may not have reached its stationary distribution yet and may need more burn-in. Figure 13.14 shows a single chain with the two segments and the Z-scores for different burn-in sizes.

In our Columbus analogy, the Geweke diagnostic compares the observations that the explorer makes in different phases of the journey. If the explorer has learned the population distribution of the city, early and late observations should give statistically similar estimates of the neighborhood populations. The early observations come after the initial familiarization, and the late ones from the end of the journey.

The Geweke diagnostic applies to individual parameters separately. This helps identify which aspects of the model have convergence issues. In complex astronomical models, some parameters often converge more slowly than others, and the diagnostic can highlight them.

The diagnostic only compares two specific segments of the chain and can therefore miss convergence issues in the middle portions. It is also sensitive to the choice of the two segments. It relies on asymptotic properties of the autocorrelation, which can be less reliable for shorter chains. The posterior may have multiple modes, and the chain may not have explored all of them. The diagnostic can then wrongly suggest convergence from a single mode.

In astronomical applications with computationally expensive models, a practical approach is to run a single long chain first.
