We use the Geweke diagnostic to check convergence and to choose the burn-in period. If resources permit, we then run several shorter chains from dispersed starting points for the final analysis and verify convergence with the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic.

The diagnostics tell us when the burn-in ends, and a good starting point makes it shorter. We can start the chain at the maximum of the posterior, which an optimizer such as gradient descent finds by minimizing the negative log posterior. This works well when the posterior has one dominant mode. The typical posterior samples can still lie some distance from the maximum, so a short burn-in remains. For the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic we then scatter the starting points of the chains around this maximum.

13.14 The Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm

The Metropolis algorithm is widely applied in astronomical research for posterior sampling. Its symmetric proposal can, however, limit the sampling efficiency in practice. This happens when the geometry of the posterior distribution is complex, for instance when parameters have different scales or are highly correlated. In such cases, we can benefit from a more general method, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.

The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm generalizes the Metropolis algorithm by dropping the symmetry requirement for the proposal distribution. It keeps detailed balance, so the target remains a stationary distribution of the chain. The Metropolis algorithm is restricted to symmetric proposals with \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) = q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')\), typically a Gaussian centered at the current position. Asymmetric proposals with \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) \neq q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')\) give more flexibility in exploring the parameter space. This becomes useful when we have prior knowledge about the geometry or the preferred directions of movement within the posterior distribution.

Consider sampling from a highly skewed distribution, such as a gamma or log-normal distribution. A symmetric Gaussian proposal needs very small steps to keep a reasonable acceptance rate in the narrow tail region. This makes the exploration of the wider region very slow. An asymmetric proposal can adapt to the local geometry, with smaller steps in the tail and larger steps in the wider region.

What we can directly control in MCMC is the transition matrix \(T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\). In both algorithms, it is the product of the proposal distribution \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})\) and the acceptance probability \(A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\), so that \[ T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}'). \]

Asymmetric proposals require an adjusted acceptance probability to maintain detailed balance. The acceptance probability of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is defined as \[ A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}\right). \]

Compared to the Metropolis algorithm, the acceptance probability has the additional factor \(q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')/q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})\). This ratio corrects for the asymmetry of the proposal distribution.

To see this intuitively, consider the Columbus explorer again. In the Metropolis algorithm, the explorer was as likely to propose traveling from the Short North to German Village as the reverse. With Metropolis-Hastings, the explorer might be more likely to propose traveling downhill than uphill, or toward the city center than away from it. The factor \(q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')/q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})\) in the acceptance probability compensates for this directional bias. Figure 13.15 shows this factor and the acceptance probability for a symmetric and an asymmetric proposal at the same current state.

Checking the Acceptance Ratio

We check detailed balance, as we did for the Metropolis algorithm. Detailed balance requires that \[ p(\mathbf{x})T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = p(\mathbf{x}')T(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}). \]

With the transition probability of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, this becomes \[ p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')A(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}). \]

The main difference from the Metropolis algorithm is the proposal distribution. The Metropolis algorithm required \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) = q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')\), so the proposal terms canceled in the acceptance ratio. Here we allow \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) \neq q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')\).

We check detailed balance in two cases. In case 1, the ratio \(p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')/(p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}))\) is at least 1. The two acceptance probabilities are then \[\begin{aligned} A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}\right) = 1 \\ A(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}\right) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}. \end{aligned}\]

Inserting these into the detailed balance equation gives \[\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) \cdot 1 &= p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}') \cdot \frac{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')} \\ p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) &= p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}), \end{aligned}\] which is true.

In case 2, the ratio \(p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')/(p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}))\) is less than 1. The two acceptance probabilities are then \[\begin{aligned} A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}\right) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})} \\ A(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}\right) = 1. \end{aligned}\]

Inserting these into the detailed balance equation gives \[\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) \cdot \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})} &= p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}') \cdot 1 \\ p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}') &= p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}'), \end{aligned}\] which is also true.

This verifies that the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm satisfies detailed balance with respect to the target posterior distribution. Like the Metropolis algorithm, it also requires the chain to be irreducible, aperiodic and positive recurrent.

In practice, astronomical applications usually satisfy these conditions, with the same caveats as for the Metropolis algorithm. It is generally advisable to use bounded priors. They keep the chain out of regions of the parameter space that are physically meaningless or computationally problematic. We should also avoid regions of zero probability in the parameter space, because they can create barriers that prevent the chain from being irreducible. When these conditions are met, the chain eventually converges to sampling from the target distribution. The long-term visitation pattern of the explorer then matches the population distribution, even though the proposals are directionally biased.

Common Special Cases

The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm has several special cases that are common in practice. The random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm uses \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) = g(\mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{x})\), where \(g\) is a distribution of steps, so it proposes the current position plus a random step. A common choice is a Gaussian \(g\) centered at zero, which gives the symmetric proposal of the Metropolis algorithm.

The independence sampler uses a proposal \(q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) = g(\mathbf{x}')\) that does not depend on the current state. The proposed state comes from the same distribution \(g\) at each step, for example a Gaussian fitted to the posterior. It can be effective when we have good prior knowledge about the target distribution, so that \(g\) resembles it.

A Langevin proposal uses gradient information from the target distribution to propose moves toward regions of higher probability. This makes it particularly effective for smooth, differentiable target distributions. The proposal is a Gaussian with step size \(\epsilon\), centered at \(\mathbf{x} + (\epsilon^2/2)\nabla \ln p(\mathbf{x})\). The gradient of the log target points toward higher probability, so the center lies uphill from \(\mathbf{x}\). Panel (b) of Figure 13.15 shows a proposal of this kind.

13.15 Gibbs Sampling

Gibbs sampling is an MCMC method that updates one parameter, or one block of parameters, at a time. The Metropolis and Metropolis-Hastings algorithms instead treat the parameter vector as a single unit. In many astronomical problems, sampling from the joint posterior \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is hard, but the conditional distributions of subsets of parameters are often tractable. We can split a parameter vector \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_D)\) into blocks, and the conditional distributions of these blocks often have standard forms that we can sample directly.

Gibbs sampling uses this structure. It breaks the high-dimensional sampling problem into a sequence of lower-dimensional sampling tasks. This is a “divide and conquer” approach, and it can improve the efficiency a great deal when the conditional distributions are well-behaved.

When the blocks are single parameters, the procedure is simple. Starting from a state \(\mathbf{x}^{(t)} = (x_1^{(t)}, x_2^{(t)}, \ldots, x_D^{(t)})\), one iteration proceeds as follows.

  • Sample \(x_1^{(t+1)} \sim p(x_1 | x_2^{(t)}, \ldots, x_D^{(t)})\)

  • Sample \(x_2^{(t+1)} \sim p(x_2 | x_1^{(t+1)}, x_3^{(t)}, \ldots, x_D^{(t)})\)

  • \(\vdots\)

  • Sample \(x_i^{(t+1)} \sim p(x_i | x_1^{(t+1)}, \ldots, x_{i-1}^{(t+1)}, x_{i+1}^{(t)}, \ldots, x_D^{(t)})\)

  • \(\vdots\)

  • Sample \(x_D^{(t+1)} \sim p(x_D | x_1^{(t+1)}, \ldots, x_{D-1}^{(t+1)})\)

Each step samples one parameter \(x_i\) directly from its conditional distribution. We use the new value at once when we condition the later parameters. Figure 13.16 shows these steps for two parameters. Sampling \(x_1\) given \(x_2\) moves the chain horizontally, and sampling \(x_2\) given the new \(x_1\) moves it vertically, so the chain follows a stair-step path.

Gibbs sampling has an advantage when the conditional distributions have standard forms, such as Gaussian, gamma or beta. Then we can use exact sampling methods, for example the inverse CDF method of Chapter 12 or special random number generators. This avoids proposal distributions and acceptance or rejection steps. If some conditional distributions have no standard form, we can apply an MCMC method to those parameters only and sample the others directly.

Gibbs Sampling as Metropolis-Hastings

It may seem puzzling that Gibbs sampling does not sample the joint distribution directly and uses only conditional distributions of blocks of parameters. We show that it works because it is a special case of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. Unlike the Metropolis algorithm, Gibbs sampling needs no arbitrary proposal distribution such as a Gaussian. It uses the conditional distributions of the target itself as the proposal. When we update the \(i\)-th component, the proposal is \[ q_i(\mathbf{x}' | \mathbf{x}) = p(x_i' | x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_D) \cdot \prod_{j \neq i} \delta(x_j' - x_j), \] where \(\delta\) is the Dirac delta function, which keeps all components except the \(i\)-th unchanged. So we propose new values only for the \(i\)-th component and draw them directly from its conditional distribution.

This proposal is valid within the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm if the acceptance probability gives detailed balance. We find the acceptance probability of this proposal from the standard Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability \[ A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}\right). \]

We evaluate this acceptance probability for the Gibbs sampler. Since we update only the \(i\)-th component, we have \(x_j' = x_j\) for all \(j \neq i\). The product rule of probability gives the joint distribution of \(\mathbf{x}\) as \[ p(\mathbf{x}) = p(x_i | x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_D) \cdot p(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_D). \] Similarly, for \(\mathbf{x}'\) we have \[ p(\mathbf{x}') = p(x_i' | x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_D) \cdot p(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_D). \]

The second factor is the same in both expressions, because all components except the \(i\)-th are the same in \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}'\). The proposal for the move from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{x}'\) is \[ q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x}) = p(x_i' | x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_D). \] The proposal for the reverse move is \[ q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}') = p(x_i | x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_D). \]

We write \(\mathbf{x}_{-i}\) for all components of \(\mathbf{x}\) except the \(i\)-th, so \(\mathbf{x}_{-i} = (x_1, \ldots,\allowbreak x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots,\allowbreak x_D)\). The conditional distributions then take the compact form \(p(x_i | \mathbf{x}_{-i})\).

Substituting these expressions into the acceptance probability gives \[\begin{aligned} A(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}')q(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}')}{p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x}'|\mathbf{x})}\right) \\ &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(x_i' | \mathbf{x}_{-i}) \cdot p(\mathbf{x}_{-i}) \cdot p(x_i | \mathbf{x}_{-i})}{p(x_i | \mathbf{x}_{-i}) \cdot p(\mathbf{x}_{-i}) \cdot p(x_i' | \mathbf{x}_{-i})}\right) \\ &= \min(1, 1) = 1. \end{aligned}\]

The acceptance probability of Gibbs sampling is 1. Standard Metropolis-Hastings uses an arbitrary proposal distribution, whereas Gibbs sampling draws each parameter from its exact conditional distribution given all the others. No rejection is needed, so Gibbs sampling is often called a “rejection-free” MCMC method.

Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings. Metropolis-Hastings satisfies detailed balance and, if the chain is ergodic, converges to the target distribution. So Gibbs sampling also converges to the posterior distribution.

Bivariate Gaussian Example

To see when Gibbs sampling works well and when it works poorly, we look at how the structure of the target distribution affects the efficiency. A bivariate Gaussian distribution is a useful example, because we can derive its conditional distributions analytically. We can also observe directly how the efficiency of Gibbs sampling varies with the correlation structure of the target. We sample from a bivariate Gaussian distribution with zero mean and correlation coefficient \(\rho\) \[ \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{bmatrix}\right). \]

Gibbs sampling needs the conditional distributions \(p(x_1 | x_2)\) and \(p(x_2 | x_1)\). For a bivariate Gaussian distribution, we can apply the standard formula for conditional distributions, which Section 5.9 derives. Suppose we have a joint Gaussian distribution \[ \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12} \\ \Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22} \end{bmatrix}\right). \]

The conditional distribution of \(x_1\) given \(x_2\) is then \[ p(x_1 | x_2) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_2 - \mu_2), \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}). \]

In our case, \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0\), \(\Sigma_{11} = \Sigma_{22} = 1\) and \(\Sigma_{12} = \Sigma_{21} = \rho\). Substituting these values gives \[\begin{aligned} p(x_1 | x_2) &= \mathcal{N}(0 + \rho \cdot 1^{-1} \cdot (x_2 - 0), 1 - \rho \cdot 1^{-1} \cdot \rho) \\ &= \mathcal{N}(\rho x_2, 1 - \rho^2). \end{aligned}\]

The last row of the display above gives the conditional distribution of \(x_1\). By symmetry, the conditional distribution of \(x_2\) is \[ p(x_2 | x_1) = \mathcal{N}(\rho x_1, 1-\rho^2). \]

These closed-form expressions make the distribution well suited to Gibbs sampling. At each step we sample directly from the conditional distributions and need no rejection step. The sampler alternates between the following two steps.

  1. Sample \(x_1^{(t+1)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\rho x_2^{(t)}, 1-\rho^2)\)

  2. Sample \(x_2^{(t+1)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\rho x_1^{(t+1)}, 1-\rho^2)\)

We vary the correlation coefficient \(\rho\) to see its effect on the efficiency of the sampler. For \(\rho = 0\), which means no correlation, the conditional distributions simplify to \[ p(x_1 | x_2) = \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \quad \text{and} \quad p(x_2 | x_1) = \mathcal{N}(0, 1). \]

The Gibbs sampler then generates independent samples in each dimension. Each conditional sampling step gives a new value unrelated to the previous samples. The chain moves through the joint distribution with high efficiency. The bivariate Gaussian has circular contours, and the sampler moves freely in both dimensions.

As \(|\rho|\) increases, the conditional relationship between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) becomes stronger. For high correlation, for example \(\rho = 0.95\), the conditional distributions become \[ p(x_1 | x_2) = \mathcal{N}(0.95 x_2, 0.0975) \quad \text{and} \quad p(x_2 | x_1) = \mathcal{N}(0.95 x_1, 0.0975). \]

The means now follow the other variable closely, and the variance drops to 0.0975, which equals \(1-\rho^2\) for \(\rho = 0.95\). The successive samples of the Gibbs sampler now have a high autocorrelation. The bivariate Gaussian has a highly elongated elliptical contour, and the sampler moves in a narrow stair-step pattern along this ellipse. The narrow pattern shows how hard it is to explore the major axis of the distribution. Figure 13.17 compares the sampling paths, the chains with their effective sample sizes and the autocorrelation functions for \(\rho = 0\) and \(\rho = 0.95\).

The case \(\rho = 0.95\) shows a limitation of standard Gibbs sampling. It can perform poorly with highly correlated parameters, which are common in astronomical models. The chain may need many iterations to explore the posterior. It then has a high autocorrelation and a low effective sample size, although the acceptance rate is 1. A rejection-free method does not guarantee efficient exploration of the parameter space.

In the Columbus analogy, a Gibbs sampler with highly correlated parameters is an explorer who can move only north-south or east-west. The important roads in the city run diagonally. Each step is valid, but the overall exploration is inefficient.

Correlated parameters lead to several strategies for improving the efficiency of Gibbs sampling. One approach is block Gibbs sampling, where we update groups of correlated parameters together rather than one at a time. In our bivariate Gaussian example, we could update \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) together instead of alternating between them. Updating them together samples directly from the joint distribution, which makes our example trivial. The example still shows a general principle, that grouping correlated parameters often lets us sample more efficiently.

Suppose we partition the parameter vector \(\mathbf{x}\) into \(B\) blocks \((\mathbf{x}_{(1)}, \mathbf{x}_{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{(B)})\). The block Gibbs sampler then proceeds as follows.

  1. Sample \(\mathbf{x}_{(1)}^{(t+1)} \sim p(\mathbf{x}_{(1)} | \mathbf{x}_{(2)}^{(t)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{(B)}^{(t)})\)

  2. Sample \(\mathbf{x}_{(2)}^{(t+1)} \sim p(\mathbf{x}_{(2)} | \mathbf{x}_{(1)}^{(t+1)}, \mathbf{x}_{(3)}^{(t)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{(B)}^{(t)})\)

  3. \(\vdots\)

  4. Sample \(\mathbf{x}_{(B)}^{(t+1)} \sim p(\mathbf{x}_{(B)} | \mathbf{x}_{(1)}^{(t+1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{(B-1)}^{(t+1)})\)

Block Gibbs sampling is also a special case of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with an acceptance probability of 1. To see this, consider the proposal distribution for updating block \(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}\) \[ q(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}^{\prime} | \mathbf{x}_{(i)}, \mathbf{x}_{(-i)}) = p(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}^{\prime} | \mathbf{x}_{(-i)}), \] where \(\mathbf{x}_{(-i)}\) represents all blocks except the \(i\)-th. The Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability, which we write \(\alpha\) here, becomes \[\begin{aligned} \alpha &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}^{\prime}, \mathbf{x}_{(-i)})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}, \mathbf{x}_{(-i)})} \cdot \frac{q(\mathbf{x}_{(i)} | \mathbf{x}_{(i)}^{\prime}, \mathbf{x}_{(-i)})}{q(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}^{\prime} | \mathbf{x}_{(i)}, \mathbf{x}_{(-i)})}\right) \\ &= \min\left(1, \frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}^{\prime} | \mathbf{x}_{(-i)}) \cdot p(\mathbf{x}_{(-i)})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{(i)} | \mathbf{x}_{(-i)}) \cdot p(\mathbf{x}_{(-i)})} \cdot \frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{(i)} | \mathbf{x}_{(-i)})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}^{\prime} | \mathbf{x}_{(-i)})}\right) \\ &= \min(1, 1) = 1. \end{aligned}\]

So the convergence result of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm carries over to block Gibbs sampling. This generalizes the single-component case to blocks of arbitrary size. The proposal is the exact conditional distribution, so the acceptance ratio simplifies to 1 and the algorithm is rejection-free.

Hierarchical Models

The conditional sampling of Gibbs sampling is well suited to hierarchical Bayesian models. In these models the parameters are organized in layers, and higher-level parameters, the hyperparameters, determine the distributions of lower-level parameters. These hyperparameters are inferred from the data, unlike those of Section 7.8, such as the learning rate, which we set before training. For example, consider a model for a population of exoplanets, where we have observations of several planetary systems. At the lowest level we have parameters for individual planets, such as masses, radii and orbital parameters. At a higher level, hyperparameters describe the population-wide distributions of these properties, such as the mean and variance of planetary masses over all systems.

The conditional structure of such models is often simple. Given the hyperparameters, the parameters of the individual planets are conditionally independent of each other, so we can update each planet without considering the others. Conditionally independent means that, once we know the hyperparameters, the parameters of one planet tell us nothing about those of another. Given the individual planet parameters, the hyperparameters typically have simple conditional distributions that depend only on the collection of individual parameters.

This structure is ideal for Gibbs sampling, which can explore the joint posterior efficiently by alternating between two steps. First, we update all individual planet parameters, possibly in parallel, because they are conditionally independent given the hyperparameters. Then we update the population hyperparameters from the current values of all individual parameters.

The same structure appears in many astronomical applications. In stellar population modeling, cluster-wide hyperparameters determine the properties of individual stars, creating a hierarchy. In galaxy clustering studies, the properties of individual galaxies depend on their host dark matter halos, forming another hierarchy. Cosmological parameter estimation often combines different probes in a hierarchical model, where Gibbs sampling can handle the complex parameter space efficiently. In these cases Gibbs sampling uses the conditional independence of the model. It is often much more efficient than generic Metropolis-Hastings, which treats all parameters as a single block.

Software and Further Methods

Astronomers rarely code these samplers from scratch, because well-tested packages implement them. Some packages run an ensemble of walkers, each of which traces its own chain. Each walker proposes steps from the positions of the other walkers, so these packages need little tuning.

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo treats the negative log posterior as a potential energy and gives each parameter a momentum. The gradient of the log posterior acts as a force, as in classical mechanics. We let this system move for a short time and propose its end point, which a Metropolis-Hastings step accepts or rejects. Because the motion nearly conserves energy, the proposal can lie far from the start and still have a high acceptance probability. Nested sampling computes the evidence and handles posteriors with several modes.

Previously intractable problems have become routine applications of MCMC. Examples are characterizing exoplanet populations, inferring cosmological parameters from several kinds of observations and modeling stellar evolution with uncertain physics. MCMC methods supply the computations behind many modeling techniques in statistics, machine learning, physics and other fields where complex probability distributions arise. The journey from the simple grid methods of Chapter 12 to the MCMC algorithms of this chapter shows a recurring theme. As problems become more complex, we must often abandon exact solutions for approximate methods that scale.

Some models still allow analytical calculations, and these are often preferable. Chapter 14 treats Gaussian processes, an advanced technique that often gives analytical solutions for the posterior predictions and the marginal likelihood (evidence). Analytical and numerical approaches each have their place in the toolkit of the modern statistician.

13.16 Tutorials: Deconvolving Noisy Data

Most posteriors in astronomy have no closed form, so we sample them with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The first of two tutorials builds the tools of this chapter, and the second uses them on noisy stellar masses. The full tutorials can be found at https://statml.org/ as 13a and 13b.

The first tutorial implements the Metropolis algorithm together with the checks that decide whether a chain can be trusted (Figure 13.18). The proposal width sets how fast the chain moves, since a narrow proposal takes tiny steps and a wide one is mostly rejected (Section 13.9). Even a well-tuned chain gives correlated samples, so the effective sample size counts how many independent samples it is worth (Section 13.11). The chain also starts away from the posterior, so we discard its first steps as burn-in. To check the burn-in, the Geweke test compares parts of one chain and the Gelman-Rubin test compares chains from different starts (Section 13.13). Finally, Gibbs sampling updates one parameter at a time without a proposal to tune, but it slows down when the parameters are correlated (Section 13.15).

The second tutorial asks how measurement errors bias the study of a population. It simulates stellar masses, each with its own error, and fits the slope of their mass function, a power law with sharp limits. The errors scatter each mass up or down, so the measured masses spread past both limits of the power law. A fit that treats them as true sees a wider, flatter distribution and finds a much shallower slope (Figure 13.19a and b). The errors bias the slope much as input errors attenuate a regression slope (Section 6.1).

To avoid this bias, the likelihood must treat the true mass of each star as unknown. If we knew it, the likelihood would be the power law at that mass. Since we do not, we consider every true mass that could have produced the measurement. Each candidate counts in proportion to how common the power law makes it and how likely its error is to give the measured value. The likelihood of a star is this average over its possible true masses.

The measurement already tells us roughly where the true mass lies, so importance sampling suits this average (Section 12.5). It draws possible true masses near the measurement and weights each by how common the power law makes it. MCMC then varies the slope, and at each step the averaged likelihood scores how well that slope explains the measured masses. Together the two account for the errors that the naive fit ignored, and the posterior contains the true slope (Figure 13.19b).

This model assumes that every star follows the power law. Real catalogs also contain unresolved binaries, which look like single stars with too high a mass. With them in the data, the chain still converges, but to a narrow posterior far below the true slope. A well-behaved chain does not guarantee a correct answer, because here the model itself is wrong. A posterior predictive check (Section 5.7) catches this, since catalogs simulated from the posterior lack the high-mass tail of the data (Figure 13.19c). A mixture model (Section 11.5) of the power law and a Gaussian for the binaries passes the check and recovers the slope.

The same approach applies to any catalog whose errors differ from object to object. Writing the likelihood in terms of the unobserved true values recovers the distribution before the errors blurred it. A posterior predictive check then tests the model itself.
